issues.legal_issue: A delayed public-interest challenge to a developmental project may be barred by laches after the project has been cleared, construction has begun, and substantial public money has been spent, except insofar as it concerns implementation of rehabilitation obligations.
material_facts: The petitioner had opposed the project for years but challenged the environmental clearance and construction only after construction had begun and substantial public funds had been spent.
The Court entertained the petition to examine whether rehabilitation measures required for protecting affected people were being implemented, but treated the other challenges as belated.
issues.conclusion: Challenges concerning the project’s height, submergence, environmental studies and clearance, hydrology, and seismicity were not entertained because they were brought too late; implementation of relief and rehabilitation remained open to scrutiny.
issues.legal_principle: Ordinary principles of laches apply to public-interest litigation. Under the Court’s approach to judicial review, a project decision cannot ordinarily be challenged after a lengthy delay during which execution and public expenditure have proceeded; the Court nevertheless may examine compliance with obligations protecting fundamental rights under Article 21 of the Constitution.

rule.if: public_interest_project_challenge and decision_known_to_challenger and construction_started and substantial_public_funds_spent and challenge_delayed and not challenge_limited_to_rehabilitation_implementation

predicates.public_interest_project_challenge: A petitioner brings a public-interest proceeding challenging a developmental project.
predicates.decision_known_to_challenger: The petitioner knew of the decision to undertake the project while there was an opportunity to challenge it earlier.
predicates.construction_started: The project authorities began construction before the challenge was filed.
predicates.substantial_public_funds_spent: Substantial public money was spent on the project before the challenge was filed.
predicates.challenge_delayed: The petitioner waited a lengthy period after learning of the decision before approaching the court.
predicates.challenge_limited_to_rehabilitation_impl: The challenge is confined to whether rehabilitation obligations for affected people are being implemented.

issues.definition: When a public-interest challenge to a known project decision is delayed until construction and substantial public spending have begun, the challenge is not entertained unless it concerns implementation of rehabilitation obligations.

issues.legal_issue: A third party cannot reopen the correctness of a final and binding published decision of an inter-State water dispute tribunal.
material_facts: A tribunal adjudicated the inter-State water dispute, including the dam’s permitted height and rehabilitation obligations.
The tribunal’s final decision was published in the Official Gazette.
The petitioner was not a State party to the water dispute and sought to challenge issues determined by the tribunal.
issues.conclusion: The petitioner could not challenge the correctness of issues decided by the tribunal, but affected people could require the States to provide the relief and resettlement directed by the award.
issues.legal_principle: Article 262 of the Constitution and Sections 5 and 6 of the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956 establish the process by which a tribunal adjudicates a water dispute and its published decision becomes final and binding on the parties. The Court relied on State of Karnataka v. State of Andhra Pradesh, 2000 (3) Scale 505, for the effect of publication and finality.

predicates.third_party_challenge_to_published_water: A person who was not a party State to an inter-State water dispute brings a proceeding challenging the tribunal’s published award.
predicates.award_final_and_binding_on_disputing_sta: The tribunal’s decision has been published and is final and binding on the States that were parties to the dispute.

issues.definition: A third party challenging a published, final water-dispute award cannot reopen the decision that binds the disputing States.

issues.legal_issue: Displacement caused by a development project does not, by itself, violate affected people’s fundamental rights when rehabilitation provides for their resettlement and improvement of their living conditions.
material_facts: The project would displace tribal and other families from homes and agricultural land.
The tribunal’s award provided for resettlement, land and house plots for qualifying families, rehabilitation grants, and civic amenities.

The States had expanded rehabilitation benefits, and the Court found that the resettlement package could provide affected families with better amenities and living conditions than those in their former settlements.
issues.conclusion: Displacement alone did not establish a violation of fundamental or other rights; the relevant concern was whether affected people were properly rehabilitated and were better off after resettlement.
issues.legal_principle: Article 21 of the Constitution protects life and human rights, and the Court accepted that international treaties may inform domestic law, referring to Gramophone Co. of India Ltd. v. B.B. Pandey, (1984) 2 SCC 534, PUCL v. Union of India, (1997) 3 SCC 433, and CERC v. Union of India, (1995) 3 SCC 42. Article 12 of ILO Convention No. 107 contemplates removal in exceptional circumstances under national law and provides for land of at least equal quality and compensation for resulting loss or injury. The Court applied these principles to the rehabilitation arrangements and did not treat displacement per se as a rights violation.

predicates.development_project_displaces_people: A public development project requires people to leave their homes or land.
predicates.rehabilitation_package_provides_resettle: The project authorities provide affected people with resettlement arrangements and basic amenities.
predicates.rehabilitation_can_improve_living_condit: The resettlement arrangements are capable of improving affected people’s living conditions compared with their former circumstances.

issues.definition: Displacement by a development project alone is not a rights violation when the affected people receive resettlement and amenities capable of improving their living conditions.

issues.legal_issue: An environmental clearance is not invalid merely because some environmental studies remain incomplete when the government consciously grants conditional clearance after consideration of available material and provides for further study and monitoring.
material_facts: Before clearance, government departments and technical bodies considered environmental information and identified studies that remained to be completed.

The government granted environmental clearance subject to conditions requiring further studies, environmental safeguards alongside project work, and completion of specified plans before reservoir filling.
An environmental sub-group headed by the Secretary of the Ministry of Environment and Forests was established to monitor safeguards.
The government continued to monitor the project, and no formal notification revoking or cancelling the clearance was issued.
issues.conclusion: The clearance was not shown to have been granted without application of mind and had not lapsed or been formally revoked.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the 1987 clearance as an administrative decision made after the relevant government consideration, with further studies and mitigation to be carried out under continuing oversight. It considered the conditions and monitoring machinery, and the absence of a formal revocation, in rejecting the challenge to the clearance.

rule.if: environmental_clearance_challenged and clearance_followed_government_consideration and further_studies_and_safeguards_required and monitoring_authority_created and no_formal_revocation

predicates.environmental_clearance_challenged: A proceeding challenges the validity or continuing effect of an environmental clearance for a project.
predicates.clearance_followed_government_considerat: The government considered available environmental information and relevant departmental views before granting clearance.
predicates.further_studies_and_safeguards_required: The clearance required further environmental studies and safeguards to be carried out as the project proceeded.
predicates.monitoring_authority_created: The government established an authority or body to monitor the environmental safeguards.
predicates.no_formal_revocation: The government did not formally revoke or cancel the clearance.

issues.definition: A conditionally granted environmental clearance remains valid where the government considered the available material, required further safeguards, established monitoring, and did not formally revoke it.

issues.legal_issue: The precautionary principle does not require a court to presume ecological disaster from a large dam where the environmental effects are known and mitigation and monitoring measures are available.
material_facts: The project was the construction of a large dam rather than a polluting industry.
The environmental changes expected from dam construction were known, and the clearance and project arrangements included environmental studies, mitigation measures, and monitoring.
The Court found no demonstrated endangered species in the impoundment area and no sufficient basis to conclude that the project would cause ecological disaster.

The petitioner sought an independent review of environmental studies and measures, but the Court found no reason to doubt the competent monitoring bodies or require independent experts to examine the studies.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not apply a presumption of ecological disaster or require the project to stop for an independent review; known environmental effects were to be addressed through mitigation and monitoring.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India, (1996) 5 SCC 647, and A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Professor M.V. Nayudu, (1999) 2 SCC 718. Where serious harm is uncertain because of inadequate information, the precautionary principle may place the burden of proof on the person proposing the potentially harmful activity. Where the project’s environmental effects are known, the Court instead considered the measures available to mitigate those effects under the principle of sustainable development. The Court distinguished the proposed dam from a polluting industry and found the cited pollution-control rule inapplicable on these facts.

rule.if: environmental_project_challenge and project_is_large_dam and environmental_effects_known and mitigation_and_monitoring_available and ecological_disaster_not_established

predicates.environmental_project_challenge: A proceeding asks a court to stop or restrict a project on environmental grounds.
predicates.project_is_large_dam: The project under challenge is the construction of a large dam rather than a polluting industry.
predicates.environmental_effects_known: The project’s likely environmental changes are sufficiently known to be assessed.
predicates.mitigation_and_monitoring_available: Measures and responsible bodies exist to address and monitor the project’s environmental effects.
predicates.ecological_disaster_not_established: The evidence does not establish that the project will cause ecological disaster.

issues.definition: Where a challenged large dam has known environmental effects, available mitigation and monitoring, and no established ecological disaster, the court does not presume disaster merely because the environment will change.

issues.legal_issue: A later statutory requirement for prior environmental clearance does not apply retrospectively to a project cleared and commenced before that requirement took effect.
material_facts: The project received environmental clearance from the Central Government before a later notification prescribed a prior-clearance procedure for listed projects.
Construction of the project had begun before that notification was issued.
issues.conclusion: The later notification did not retrospectively govern the project or invalidate the earlier clearance.
issues.legal_principle: The Court interpreted the notification made under Section 3(1) and Section 3(2)(v) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, read with Rule 5(3)(d) of the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986, as prospective. It held that the later prior-clearance procedure could not be applied retrospectively to a project already cleared and under construction.

predicates.prior_project_clearance_regime_challenge: A proceeding argues that a later prior-clearance requirement governs an existing project.
predicates.project_cleared_before_new_prior_clearan: The project received government clearance before the later prior-clearance requirement took effect.
predicates.construction_started_before_new_requirem: Construction of the project began before the later requirement took effect.

issues.definition: A later prior-clearance requirement does not retrospectively govern a project cleared and under construction before that requirement took effect.

issues.legal_issue: Courts should not substitute their judgment for a considered government policy decision to undertake a major infrastructure project unless the decision involves illegality, bad faith, or a violation of fundamental rights.
material_facts: The project had been considered over an extended period by the Union Government and multiple States, and an inter-State tribunal had determined the dispute and the project parameters.
The project had received government and Planning Commission consideration, and construction had commenced.
The government had considered competing public benefits and displacement concerns, and the Court found no material establishing bad faith or a basis to fault the project decision.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to review the project decision as a policy choice and held that the project should proceed unless a blatant illegality in its undertaking or execution was shown.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the constitutional division between executive policy-making and judicial review. Courts may ensure that government action does not violate law or impermissibly transgress fundamental rights, but should not act as an approval authority or sit in appeal over a considered policy decision among competing options. The Court also applied the principles concerning laches in public-interest litigation described above.

rule.if: judicial_review_of_infrastructure_policy and considered_government_decision and project_execution_started and no_blantant_illegality_or_bad_faith_shown

predicates.judicial_review_of_infrastructure_policy: A proceeding asks a court to reconsider the government’s choice to undertake or execute major infrastructure.
predicates.considered_government_decision: The responsible government considered the project and competing interests before deciding to proceed.
predicates.project_execution_started: The project had moved from policy decision to execution before the court was asked to intervene.
predicates.no_blantant_illegality_or_bad_faith_show: The proceeding does not establish blatant illegality or bad faith in the project’s undertaking or execution.

issues.definition: A court does not replace a considered government choice about infrastructure with its own policy judgment when execution has begun and blatant illegality or bad faith is not shown.

issues.legal_issue: A shortfall in rehabilitation measures under a binding inter-State project award calls for enforcement of those obligations, not suspension of the project, while further construction must proceed alongside rehabilitation and environmental clearances.
material_facts: The binding tribunal award authorized the project and prescribed relief and rehabilitation measures, including a requirement that affected people be rehabilitated before submergence.
The States had established project authorities, rehabilitation and environmental sub-groups, grievance redressal authorities, and a review committee to oversee performance.

Rehabilitation progress was uneven, particularly in one State, while the responsible sub-group had cleared construction to a specified stage and further raising of the dam required additional clearances.
The Court found that continued monitoring and directions to the States could ensure implementation of rehabilitation and environmental safeguards.
issues.conclusion: Construction was permitted to continue to the stage already cleared, with further raising allowed only alongside implementation of rehabilitation and after rehabilitation and environmental clearances; the States were directed to implement the award and the project authorities were to monitor and enforce compliance.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 6 of the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956, a published tribunal decision is final and binding on the States. The Court held that the proper judicial response to a State’s failure to perform rehabilitation obligations is to direct implementation of the award, rather than stop the project. Article 21 requires protection of affected people’s rights, and the Court relied on the monitoring approach in B.D. Sharma v. Union of India, 1992 Supp. (3) SCC 93, while imposing staged rehabilitation and environmental oversight.

rule.if: project_implementation_challenge and binding_award_requires_rehabilitation and rehabilitation_progress_is_incomplete_or_uneven and monitoring_and_clearance_mechanisms_exist

predicates.project_implementation_challenge: A proceeding challenges the continued execution of a project governed by an inter-State award.
predicates.binding_award_requires_rehabilitation: A binding award authorizes the project and requires relief and rehabilitation for affected people.
predicates.rehabilitation_progress_is_incomplete_or: The States have not yet completed rehabilitation uniformly for all affected people.
predicates.monitoring_and_clearance_mechanisms_exis: Authorities exist to monitor rehabilitation and environmental measures and to clear further stages of construction.

issues.definition: When an award requires rehabilitation, implementation is incomplete, and monitoring mechanisms exist, the project continues only in stages linked to rehabilitation and environmental clearances.
